title: Old Books Likely Being Destroyed to Train AI
paragraphs: Over the last few months, used bookstores around the world have seen significant spikes in sales.

For many, it started around April. They don't know who is buying the books, however. They're being ordered in bulk by large online marketplaces like Biblio, which will receive the books at a warehouse, then send them to the actual buyer.
But many booksellers think they're being bought to teach AI.

We know that Anthropic, maker of the AI chatbot Claude, has been doing exactly that. A 2025 court case in San Francisco revealed that the company had bought millions of print books to train its systems. It was also destroying those books, cutting the bindings off to make the pages easier — and cheaper — to scan.
Anthropic was sued for using those books without the authors' permission. But the judge ruled that it's fine for Anthropic's AI to learn by reading books, just as it's fine for humans to do so.

And older printed books, especially on niche topics, are particularly valuable to AI companies — because the text is probably difficult to find online, if it's there at all. More importantly, if the book was printed before 2022, all of it will have been written by a human — keeping AI safe from "learning" from content it produced itself.
However, it looks bad for AI companies to be destroying books — even if Anthropic has promised that it doesn't buy or destroy rare volumes. So they're ordered anonymously.

This has even hit Japan, where Nippon News Network reports that online used bookstores have seen a big spike in bulk sales since August, with many books apparently going to a logistics center in Okayama prefecture.

Documents in the Anthropic case also mentioned a contract with "Nippan Japan." And in October, Nippan Group Holdings, a major Japanese book distributor, admitted that one of its subsidiaries sold books to Anthropic between December 2024 and December 2025 — though it also said it had not known the books were intended for AI learning.
